blogs.title: Fair Use at the Pleading Stage, Revisited: Why Santos v. Kimmel Makes Early Dismissal Look Increasingly Normal
blogs.description: This post would examine the Second Circuit’s willingness to affirm fair use on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, emphasizing the court’s reliance on the works themselves, the complaint, and judicially noticeable copyright registrations. It would situate Santos v. Kimmel within Second Circuit precedent like TCA Television, Cariou, Authors Guild, and Hachette, and ask whether the decision signals a broader trend toward resolving obvious parody/commentary cases early—thereby reducing litigation costs but also narrowing discovery opportunities for copyright plaintiffs.

blogs.title: From Warhol to Kimmel: Objective Purpose, Not Authorial Intent, Drives Transformative Use
blogs.description: This post would focus on the opinion’s treatment of the first fair use factor and its insistence that transformative purpose is judged from the standpoint of a reasonable observer, not the copyright owner’s asserted intentions. The blog would explore how the panel uses the Supreme Court’s Warhol decision to reject Santos’s argument that he and Kimmel shared the same basic purpose, and would analyze the doctrinal tension between user purpose, audience perception, and the growing importance of criticism and commentary as paradigmatic transformative uses.

blogs.title: Bad Faith Without Consequence? Santos v. Kimmel and the Declining Role of Deception in Fair Use
blogs.description: This post would analyze the panel’s treatment of Kimmel’s use of fictitious identities to procure the Cameo videos. It would explore how the court acknowledges Harper & Row’s language that fair use 'presupposes good faith' but effectively relegates bad faith to the margins where the use is plainly critical and non-substitutive. The piece would consider whether Santos v. Kimmel further weakens bad faith as an independent limit on fair use, especially in cases involving media stings, undercover acquisition, or platform-mediated trickery.

blogs.title: Copyright Preemption Dodged, Contract Law Enforced Strictly: The Quiet State-Law Lessons of Santos v. Kimmel
blogs.description: This post would turn away from fair use and examine the state-law holdings. It would explain why the Second Circuit declined to resolve the preemption question and instead disposed of the claims on ordinary contract and fraud principles: Santos was not a third-party beneficiary of Cameo’s Terms of Service under Illinois law, failed to plead essential terms or mutual assent for an implied contract under New York law, and alleged no out-of-pocket loss for fraudulent inducement. The post would highlight the practical lesson for creators who try to repackage failed copyright claims as platform-contract or fraud actions.
